claims.claim: adult annual mortality A 0.37–0.59 at ages IV+ in the Patuxent River, Maryland
claims.location: p. 184 (PDF p. 74), text and Table 26; abstract p. 142 (PDF p. 32)
claims.quote: Among males, the annual probability of dying ranged from 0.37 to 0.59
claims.conditions: catch curves (unweighted lag differences) by year of collection, 1948–55: males 0.37–0.59, females 0.38–0.59; pooled 1948–55 estimates 0.50 for males and 0.56 for females after age group IV; an exploited estuarine population (commercial nets and angling, 8-in legal minimum); 3,475 fish aged from scales
claims.note: The range spans the yearly estimates; the pooled values (0.50 males, 0.56 females) are the better single numbers. Mansueti notes that the unexploited fish under age V had a slightly lower probability of dying than exploited older fish. The life expectancy after age IV was 'slightly more than 1½ years'.

claims.claim: stunting in white perch has been tied to density (Mansueti 1961)
claims.location: p. 195 (PDF p. 85), Discussion; p. 190 (PDF p. 80); p. 169 (PDF p. 59); abstract p. 142
claims.quote: overcrowding produces stunting in growth, undercrowding or sparse populations demonstrate greater than average growth
claims.conditions: the evidence: back-calculated first-year growth of the 1942–50 year-classes was negatively correlated with an indirect index of abundance, the Patuxent commercial haul-seine catch of 1947–55, five years later when each year-class entered the fishery (r = −0.753, P < 0.01; Fig. 15, p. 169); Mansueti attributes it to intraspecific competition for food
claims.note: For the slow-growing ('stunted') fish of the upper Patuxent he says the cause, culling by size, food shortage or high density, 'is unknown' (p. 190). The density link rests on a correlation with a catch index, not on measured densities; 'tied to density' is fair, 'shown to be caused by density' would not be.

notes: Useful for Hot Brook: Mansueti compares growth with Maine (Cooper 1941; Fuller & Cooper) and finds the Maryland curve overlaps Maine's, but 'the average life span of Maine white perch is about 7 years, while it is about 4 years in Maryland'; Maine fish reached 16 years, Maryland none over 10 (p. 189). Maturity: 50 % of males at 100.3 mm and females at 105.5 mm SL; all males from age II and all females above age IV mature. Spawning late March–May at 10–15 °C in tidal and non-tidal fresh and slightly brackish water. First-year growth was positively related to the number of spring days at 10–15 °C and to February–June solar radiation, negatively to February–May rainfall. The tagged population (3,024 tagged, 10.7 % recaptured) was essentially self-contained within the estuary.
